EDITORIAL: Endorsement: No on Props. 40, 41 and 42. Reject billionaires tax -- and billionaires' attempts to shackle state's fiscal future.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
Updated October 21, 2026 5:42 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Successive waves of federal cuts to California's safety net are hitting our shores - and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California's Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state's safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 - countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state's fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It's the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here's how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state's 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised - estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert - would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn't just that it's targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They're difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn't fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley's largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California's extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state's income taxes.
For that reason, the state's most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst's Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will "probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax," according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That's because the LAO worries that "billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away."
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state's General Fund revenues by "less than a billion per year."
But the union that pushed this proposition - Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West - wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they'll suffer when the state's General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
"We can't let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state's tax code on its own terms," said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn't agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California - a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt - created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won't take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative's requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor's recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the "Gann Limit" - a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with - six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties - think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI's development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley's latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom's beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era's technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.

# My recommendation: **NO**

After researching the official voter guide, the full legal text, the Legislative Analyst's analysis, campaign finance records, fact-checks, and editorial positions, here's what I found and why I'd vote no.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Despite its official framing as the "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act," every independent analysis — the LAO, CalMatters, Berkeley IGS — describes Prop 42 as a **countermeasure designed to nullify Prop 40**, the "billionaire tax" (a one-time 5% tax on ~200 Californians worth over $1 billion, funding healthcare). The measure's own text contains a "conflicting measures" clause explicitly voiding Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more votes. It would also permanently ban any new state tax on the ownership of personal property (stocks, bonds, business interests, art, etc.) and most retroactive taxes.

## Key findings that drove my decision

1. **The problem it advertises doesn't exist.** There is no tax — and no live proposal — on ordinary Californians' 401(k)s, pensions, or savings. California taxes retirement funds at withdrawal (following federal rules), and all six wealth tax bills introduced since 2019 died in the Legislature without a single floor vote. The one real wealth tax on the ballot (Prop 40) applies only to billionaires and *exempts* retirement accounts. CalMatters rated the "they'll expand it to everyone" claim only "partially true," noting it's written into the constitution and expansion would require another vote of the people.

2. **It was bought and paid for by the people it protects.** Prop 42 was drafted and funded by Building a Better California, bankrolled by ~$102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin (whose estimated tax bill under Prop 40 is ~$13 billion), plus Doerr, Khosla, and others. # My recommendation: **NO**

After researching the official voter guide, the full legal text, the Legislative Analyst's analysis, campaign finance records, fact-checks, and editorial positions, here's what I found and why I'd vote no.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Despite its official framing as the "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act," every independent analysis — the LAO, CalMatters, Berkeley IGS — describes Prop 42 as a **countermeasure designed to nullify Prop 40**, the "billionaire tax" (a one-time 5% tax on ~200 Californians worth over $1 billion, funding healthcare). The measure's own text contains a "conflicting measures" clause explicitly voiding Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more votes. It would also permanently ban any new state tax on the ownership of personal property (stocks, bonds, business interests, art, etc.) and most retroactive taxes.

## Key findings that drove my decision

1. **The problem it advertises doesn't exist.** There is no tax — and no live proposal — on ordinary Californians' 401(k)s, pensions, or savings. California taxes retirement funds at withdrawal (following federal rules), and all six wealth tax bills introduced since 2019 died in the Legislature without a single floor vote. The one real wealth tax on the ballot (Prop 40) applies only to billionaires and *exempts* retirement accounts. CalMatters rated the "they'll expand it to everyone" claim only "partially true," noting it's written into the constitution and expansion would require another vote of the people.

2. **It was bought and paid for by the people it protects.** Prop 42 was drafted and funded by Building a Better California, bankrolled by ~$102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin (whose estimated tax bill under Prop 40 is ~$13 billion), plus Doerr, Khosla, and others. Opposition spending is outraising supporters roughly 9-to-1 — one of the most expensive initiative fights in California history.

3. **It's redundant for anyone who opposes the billionaire tax.** If you dislike Prop 40, you can simply vote no on Prop 40. Prop 42's only added value is *permanently* amending the constitution to ban wealth taxation — locking in a policy preference written by and for the ultra-wealthy, during an era of historic (and possibly AI-accelerated) wealth concentration.

4. **Even Prop 40's critics reject Prop 42.** The Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, and the LA Times's Skelton all recommend no — with several saying they oppose the billionaire tax but won't stomach the deceptive poison-pill tactic. Their common thread: don't reward ballot measures that paper over their real purpose by stoking phantom fears about your retirement account.

## The honest case for the other side

If your overriding goal is to make a wealth tax constitutionally impossible forever — and you're comfortable with billionaires writing that rule themselves — then Yes is the coherent vote. Gov. Newsom, the firefighters and building trades unions, and the U-T/OC Register editorial boards take that position, citing capital-flight risk and double-taxation concerns. Those are legitimate arguments about Prop 40 itself, but they're arguments for voting on Prop 40 directly, not for this measure.

**Bottom line: Vote NO.** A measure sold as protecting your savings that actually exists to shield ~200 billionaires from a one-time tax — funded by those same billionaires at a 9-to-1 spending advantage — and that would permanently entrench its drafters' preferences in the constitution, fails the smell test. The straightforward way to oppose the billionaire tax is a no vote on Prop 40, not a deceptive constitutional amendment.

5. **Deceptive-ballot-measure precedent**: Rewarding poison-pill measures designed to confuse voters (which measure gets more votes wins) encourages more of them.
6. **Editorial consensus**: Even papers that oppose the billionaire tax (Sac Bee/Mercury News/East Bay Times, LA Times' Skelton) say No on 42. Only the more conservative U-T and OCR say Yes, on philosophical limited-tax grounds.

Weighing: The strongest Yes argument is philosophical (wealth taxes are bad, ban them forever). But the measure's deceptive framing, billionaire self-dealing, phantom-threat marketing, and permanent constitutional lock-in tilt heavily toward No for an undecided voter. The key logical point: voting No on Prop 42 doesn't impose any tax — the actual tax question is decided separately on Prop 40. Prop 42 is only needed if you fear future wealth taxes, which the Legislature has repeatedly rejected and which would face voters anyway.

Also the fairness point cuts both ways: Prop 42 itself nullifies a measure voters might pass, using a vote-counting trick engineered so that people who want to "protect retirement" inadvertently kill the billionaire tax.

# My recommendation: **NO**

After researching the official voter guide, the full legal text, the Legislative Analyst's analysis, campaign finance records, fact-checks, and editorial positions, here's what I found and why I'd vote no.

## What Prop 42 actually is

Despite its official framing as the "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act," every independent analysis — the LAO, CalMatters, Berkeley IGS — describes Prop 42 as a **countermeasure designed to nullify Prop 40**, the "billionaire tax" (a one-time 5% tax on ~200 Californians worth over $1 billion, funding healthcare). The measure's own text contains a "conflicting measures" clause explicitly voiding Prop 40 if Prop 42 gets more votes. It would also permanently ban any new state tax on the ownership of personal property (stocks, bonds, business interests, art, etc.) and most retroactive taxes.

## Key findings that drove my decision

1. **The problem it advertises doesn't exist.** There is no tax — and no live proposal — on ordinary Californians' 401(k)s, pensions, or savings. California taxes retirement funds at withdrawal (following federal rules), and all six wealth tax bills introduced since 2019 died in the Legislature without a single floor vote. The one real wealth tax on the ballot (Prop 40) applies only to billionaires and *exempts* retirement accounts. CalMatters rated the "they'll expand it to everyone" claim only "partially true," noting it's written into the constitution and expansion would require another vote of the people.

2. **It was bought and paid for by the people it protects.** Prop 42 was drafted and funded by Building a Better California, bankrolled by ~$102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin (whose estimated tax bill under Prop 40 is ~$13 billion), plus Doerr, Khosla, and others. Opposition spending is outraising supporters roughly 9-to-1 — one of the most expensive initiative fights in California history.

3. **It's redundant for anyone who opposes the billionaire tax.** If you dislike Prop 40, you can simply vote no on Prop 40. Prop 42's only added value is *permanently* amending the constitution to ban wealth taxation — locking in a policy preference written by and for the ultra-wealthy, during an era of historic (and possibly AI-accelerated) wealth concentration.

4. **Even Prop 40's critics reject Prop 42.** The Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, and the LA Times's Skelton all recommend no — with several saying they oppose the billionaire tax but won't stomach the deceptive poison-pill tactic. Their common thread: don't reward ballot measures that paper over their real purpose by stoking phantom fears about your retirement account.

## The honest case for the other side

If your overriding goal is to make a wealth tax constitutionally impossible forever — and you're comfortable with billionaires writing that rule themselves — then Yes is the coherent vote. Gov. Newsom, the firefighters and building trades unions, and the U-T/OC Register editorial boards take that position, citing capital-flight risk and double-taxation concerns. Those are legitimate arguments about Prop 40 itself, but they're arguments for voting on Prop 40 directly, not for this measure.

**Bottom line: Vote NO.** A measure sold as protecting your savings that actually exists to shield ~200 billionaires from a one-time tax — funded by those same billionaires at a 9-to-1 spending advantage — and that would permanently entrench its drafters' preferences in the constitution, fails the smell test. The straightforward way to oppose the billionaire tax is a no vote on Prop 40, not a deceptive constitutional amendment.

Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Certain Personal Property Is Taxed in California. Both the state and local governments tax the ownership of certain personal property. These taxes are based on the property’s value. Personal property is all the things that people own other than real estate. One example of these kinds of taxes is the vehicle license fee that car and truck owners pay to the Department of Motor Vehicles each year. Another example is the property taxes owners of business equipment pay to the county each year.
Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed. The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed. One major example is financial assets like stocks and investment accounts. Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
PROPOSAL
Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property. Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
Limits Retroactive Taxes. Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively. A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past. An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future. Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future. This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes. This could reduce future tax revenues. When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.

PROP
42
PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
YES ON PROP. 42: PROTECT YOUR RETIREMENT AND LIFE SAVINGS FROM STATE TAXES
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. Every year, higher costs and taxes make it harder to save. An April 2026 survey found 73% of Californians know someone who has had to delay retirement for financial reasons.
CALIFORNIA CONSTITUTION CURRENTLY ALLOWS DOUBLE TAXATION
Yet, California’s Constitution currently allows the Legislature to tax the value of our personal property like retirement funds and savings accounts, even though residents already pay income tax on that money when they earn it. This means politicians can tax the same money twice: once when you earn it, and again when it is sitting in your retirement funds or savings accounts. That’s double taxation!
In the last few years alone, the Legislature and special interests have introduced six separate proposals that would tax retirement and savings accounts.
Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California-we need protections against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS
Prop. 42 amends the state Constitution to protect Californians from this double taxation by special interests and politicians. Specifically, the measure:
• Prohibits new taxes on personal property, such as retirement funds, pensions and savings accounts; • Prohibits retroactive taxes; and • Prohibits all new taxes on retirement and savings this year and in the future.
PROP. 42 PROTECTS ALL FORMS OF RETIREMENT FUNDS AND SAVINGS FROM NEW TAXES
Roughly 80% of Californians report having some form of retirement fund or savings, including young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; and retirees who depend on their savings for financial security.
This measure protects all forms of personal property from new taxes, including 401ks, pensions, IRAs and personal savings.
“Prop. 42 protects Californians’ savings and retirement. Whether it’s a union member’s hard-earned pension or a small business owner’s IRA, new taxes on retirement shouldn’t stand between people and the security they’ve planned for.” -Chris Hannan, President, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California representing hundreds of thousands of union construction trades workers.
PROP. 42 PROHIBITS UNFAIR RETROACTIVE TAXES
The state should not be able to pass new taxes that apply retroactively to money that taxpayers earned in the past. Prop. 42 requires any new taxes to apply only after voters have approved them.
“It’s a question of fairness and common sense. People plan their retirement for years-they deserve stable, predictable rules that don’t change after years of saving and planning. Prop. 42 provides that certainty.” -Sean Morgan, licensed financial advisor
Prop. 42 is supported by a broad coalition of seniors, veterans, small business owners, blue-collar workers, retirees, including groups like the California Professional Firefighters and Disabled American Veterans, Dept. of California.
Californians are already struggling with high costs of living and high taxes. Many work their entire lives to achieve some measure of retirement security. It should be illegal for politicians and special interests to tax our retirement and savings.
You earned and saved it. Now we need to protect it. Please join us in voting Yes on 42. YesonProp42.org
Michael Hedges , President
California Small Business Association
Shelley Huff , Commander
AMVETS, Department of California
Jennifer Yoder , Board Member
California Senior Alliance
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 42
THIS IS ANOTHER BILLIONAIRE-FUNDED TRICK
Don’t be fooled-Prop. 42 is not really about protecting your retirement savings from new taxes.
It’s a redundant, expensive trick to allow approximately 200 billionaires to keep avoiding paying their own taxes while YOU get stuck with the bill.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 is a billionaire-funded scheme designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. They’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
WHO’S BEHIND THIS? SOME OF DONALD TRUMP’S DONORS
The billionaires behind this don’t care about protecting your retirement savings. They’re protecting themselves. They’ve been getting out of paying their own taxes for years through loopholes and tax breaks.
This sham initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
PROP. 40 WOULD ONLY TAX BILLIONAIRES’ $2 TRILLION IN WEALTH
The billionaires behind Prop. 42 have spread lies about the California Billionaire Tax (Prop. 40), trying to trick voters into thinking that their retirement and savings are at risk.
Don’t buy the fear-mongering. The California Billionaires Tax ONLY applies to billionaires. It’s about making billionaires finally pay their fair share so we’re not stuck with shuttered hospitals and skyrocketing healthcare costs.
Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 42
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42. This is a billionaire-funded initiative designed specifically to undo the California Billionaire Tax, Prop. 40.
PROP. 42 WOULD CANCEL OUT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
Prop. 42 was put on the ballot for one reason-because billionaires don’t want to pay their fair share. This initiative was created to trick voters like you into making a billionaire tax impossible to enforce. That’s why you must vote NO.
Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Prop. 42 isn’t about preventing new taxes on personal property. It’s about preventing one specific tax that billionaires want to avoid, because they’d rather millions of working people lose healthcare than pay a modest, one-time tax on their extreme wealth.
PROP. 42 WAS FUNDED BY BILLIONAIRES WHO WANT YOU TO PAY MORE FOR HEALTHCARE
One of Prop. 42’s main funders is Google founder and Trump donor Sergey Brin, whose wealth has DOUBLED to nearly $300 billion since Trump’s election. Now he’s spent over $57 million to fund sham measures like Prop. 42 that attempt to cancel out a billionaire tax. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders called this arrogant move by Brin “unacceptable.”
Donald Trump took money out of working peoples’ pockets and gave it to billionaires like Brin through massive tax breaks. Now, the billionaires backing Prop. 42 want YOU to pay more for your healthcare.
VOTE NO ON PROP. 42 IF YOU SUPPORT THE BILLIONAIRE TAX
We have a chance to make billionaires pay their fair share to keep hospitals open and healthcare affordable for California’s working families. Vote NO on Prop. 42.
Suzanne Jimenez , Chief of Staff
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 42
WHO SUPPORTS PROP. 42
Prop. 42 is supported by hundreds of thousands of seniors, veterans, firefighters, blue-collar workers, public-safety officers and working families because it protects the retirement and savings of ALL Californians from new taxes. Who opposes 42? One organization that wants to tax retirement accounts.
WHY WE NEED PROP. 42
Sacramento politicians and special interests have repeatedly tried to pass taxes on retirement and personal savings accounts in recent years. They’ve relied on a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows government to tax our income when we earn it, and AGAIN when it is simply sitting in our savings and retirement accounts.
CALIFORNIA IS EXPENSIVE ENOUGH WITHOUT DOUBLE TAXATION
Prop. 42 prohibits this double taxation by PROHIBITING ALL NEW TAXES ON RETIREMENT AND SAVINGS ACCOUNTS and other personal property, whether proposed by legislation or ballot measure, including proposals on this year’s ballot and in the future.
It is a comprehensive constitutional protection against politicians or special interests trying to tax our retirement funds and savings accounts.
WHO BENEFITS FROM PROP. 42
Prop. 42 protects the retirement and savings for all Californians-young workers just beginning to save; teachers, firefighters and police officers with pensions; retirees and veterans who depend on their savings for financial security.
You saved it. You deserve to keep it.
Prop. 42 asks a simple question: should California politicians have the power to tax your personal property, including retirement and savings accounts?
If you think your retirement and savings should be protected from taxes, vote Yes on 42.
Darrell Roberts , President
California Professional Firefighters
Chris Hannan , President
State Building and Construction Trades Council of California
Brian R. Marvel , President
Peace Officers Research Association of California

IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

Now I have the picture:
- Prop 40: The "California Billionaire Tax" - 5% one-time wealth tax on billionaires (>$1B assets), revenue primarily for healthcare. Sponsored by SEIU-UHW and Bernie Sanders.
- Prop 41: Nullifies state taxes enacted after Jan 1, 2026 that exempt revenues from state spending limit; requires audits. Funded by the same billionaires (Sergey Brin's $57M). Designed to undo Prop 40 because Prop 40 exempts its revenues from the spending limit.
- Prop 42: Prohibits new taxes on personal property (which includes financial assets/wealth) and retroactive taxes. Prop 40 is arguably a personal property tax on wealth (a 5% tax on wealth based on past activities — potentially retroactive). Designed to undo Prop 40 too.

So Props 41 and 42 are both billionaire-funded counter-measures to Prop 40. Sergey Brin has reportedly spent ~$57 million.

Now let me research:
1. News coverage: LA Times, SF Chronicle, CalMatters, Sacramento Bee endorsements/analyses
2. The exact text of Prop 42 to understand its breadth (does it only affect billionaires? It would prohibit ALL new state taxes on personal property ownership — which effectively forecloses any wealth tax)
3. Funding details (who's paying)
4. Who supports/opposes
5. Editorial positions

Let me also check the LAO full analysis which might be more detailed than the voter guide version, and get the text of the proposed law.

Key question for my recommendation: Is Prop 42 a good idea on its merits?

Arguments for Yes:
- Prohibits double taxation of savings/retirement
- Prevents retroactive taxation
- Protects ordinary Californians' savings

Arguments for No:
- California currently does NOT tax savings/retirement ownership; there's no realistic proposal to do so for ordinary people. Prop 40 only taxes billionaires.
- The main real-world effect is to nullify the billionaire tax (Prop 40)
- Funded by billionaires (Sergey Brin, $57M+) to protect their own wealth
- Could permanently foreclose wealth taxation as a policy tool
- The "double taxation" argument is misleading: wealth taxes tax unrealized gains that have never been taxed
- Retroactive tax prohibition — Prop 40 is structured as applying to wealth accumulated in the past

PROHIBITS NEW STATE PERSONAL PROPERTY TAXES AND CERTAIN RETROACTIVE STATE TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. subclause, sentence, phrase, word, and application not
declared invalid or unconstitutional without regard to
whether any part of this act or application thereof

PROPOSED LAW
SECTION 1. Title.
This act shall be known, and may be cited, as the
Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act of
2026.
SEC. 2. Findings and Declarations.
(a) California families are paying more for everything
and we already pay some of the highest taxes in the
country. A recent analysis by a nonpartisan research
institute concluded that California ranks 3rd worst in
the nation in subjecting its population to taxes when
considering individual income taxes, sales taxes,
property taxes, and other forms of taxation. California is
behind only New Jersey and the District of Columbia in
this regard. California also has the highest state sales
TEXT OF PROPOSED LAWS PROPOSITION 42 CONTINUED
tax in the nation, the highest top income tax rate, and
the highest tax on gasoline, among other indicators.
(b) Every day, Californians are also facing an
affordability crisis. Costs for housing, food, electricity,
health care, home and auto insurance, and many other
life necessities continue to escalate. Californians are
struggling economically just to make ends meet on a
daily basis. Saving for retirement or a rainy day is even
harder. Given the state’s extraordinarily high cost of
living, a recent analysis suggests that Californians
would need $2.3 million saved up if they want to retire
comfortably for 20 years. This is an impossible sum for
many Californians.
(c) To make matters worse, politicians and special
interest groups want to start taxing retirement holdings,
individually owned assets, and other forms of personal
savings—even though the “California Dream” is getting
further out of reach for many of us and many
Californians struggle to save enough money to retire.
Here is just some of what could be at risk:
(1) Teachers, police officers, firefighters, and other
dedicated workers earn defined-benefit pension
benefits. They could be taxed on the future value of
their pension benefits and forced to pay the
government before they ever collect a dime in pension
pay.
(2) Californians who contribute to 401(k) retirement
plans and individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and
invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other
investments could be taxed on the value of their
retirement nest eggs. This could cost workers some of
their hard-earned savings, causing them to put off
retirement and leaving them more economically
vulnerable later in life.
(d) California already imposes income taxes, capital
gains taxes, real property taxes, personal property
taxes, corporation taxes, sales and use taxes, real
property transaction taxes and many other taxes on its
residents. In addition, once Californians begin to
access their retirement holdings, sell their individually
owned assets, or realize the growth in other personal
savings, they are already subject to the state’s income,
capital gains, and property taxes. But politicians and
special interests should be prohibited from taxing the
mere ownership or control of personal property such as
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings that Californians work
hard to save.
(e) Retroactive taxes can have the same devastating
effects on Californians’ retirement planning and
personal savings. Fundamental principles of fairness in
a democratic society require that individuals, families,
and businesses be able to understand and rely upon
the tax laws that govern their financial planning so they
can make decisions with advance notice of what the
rules are.
(f) The ability of Californians to organize and achieve
their financial and retirement goals depends on having
advance notice of the tax obligations that apply to
them. Retroactive changes to tax laws are
fundamentally unfair and undermine confidence in
government, disrupt retirement and financial planning,
and prevent residents and businesses from preparing
for the future.
(g) Sacramento politicians and special interests have
wasted billions of our tax dollars on inefficient and
ineffective programs. But they keep coming back for
more of our money with more tax proposals. They don’t
need to tax our retirement holdings or tax us
retroactively based on past conduct, activities, or
status—they need to deliver better results with what
taxpayers have already given them to spend.
SEC. 3. Statement of Purpose.
In enacting this act, the purpose and intent of the
people of the State of California is to protect
Californians’ ability to save for their futures by
prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal
property, including the ownership or control of
retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and
other forms of personal savings as well as requiring all
new taxes to only apply prospectively.
SEC. 4. Article VIII is added to the California
Constitution, to read:
ARTICLE VIII
SECTION 1. Prohibition on Taxing Retirement Holdings,
Individually Owned Assets, and Other Forms of Personal
Savings
(a) No state law and no provision of this Constitution
enacted on or after January 1, 2026, may enact, create,
impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership
or control of retirement holdings, individually owned
assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether
held directly or indirectly.

Endorsement: Is California coming for your retirement account? That’s what Prop 42 asks you to believe
Prop 42 is the second of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
Is California coming for your retirement account?
That’s what the backers of Proposition 42 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop42-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot would have you believe. Their measure would prohibit new state taxes on personal property — such as stocks and retirement accounts (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop42-110326.pdf) — and other forms of asset ownership, while also banning certain retroactive state taxes.
Evan McLaughlin, political director for the California Professional Firefighters, which represents firefighter unions across the state, told the editorial board in an endorsement interview that Prop 42 adds important protections for working families. In recent years, Democratic state lawmakers have introduced a handful of wealth tax proposals targeting the rich. But once you take the lid off a new form of taxation, he argued, there’s nothing stopping it from spreading to the rest of us.
“The Legislature isn’t going to wall themselves off from doing this,” McLaughlin said. “We think that it’s a public benefit to people to say, ‘If you’re going to try to tax these types of retirement assets and 401(k)s and personal savings, you need to go to a vote of the people.’”

That certainly sounds reasonable. But no one is coming for your 401(k).
California largely follows (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=17501) the federal government’s framework for evaluating pensions and retirement accounts — taxing funds when they’re withdrawn, not when they’re deposited — and there are no concerted efforts to change that.
In reality, Prop 42 is just another poison-pill measure aimed at killing Prop 40, the billionaire wealth tax.
The measure is backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php). And it explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 42 (or its cousin Prop 41 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-california-prop-41-taxes-22445889.php)) passes with more votes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s true Prop 40 does add a potentially concerning new wrinkle by including Roth IRAs and “substantially similar” accounts worth more than $10 million in its formula for taxable wealth. David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and one of Prop 42’s opponents, pointed to a ProPublica investigation (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) that found Peter Thiel and other billionaires have quietly used Roth IRAs to amass gargantuan tax-exempt fortunes.
But Prop 40 specifically excludes (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) qualified pensions and retirement accounts (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:26+section:219+edition:prelim)#:~:text=(5)%20Active%20participant), including 401(k)s, from being considered as “assets.”
There is little merit in adding yet another ballot-box budgeting rule to California’s already head-spinning list of restrictions. Lawmakers have already killed all six wealth tax proposals introduced since 2019; none made it out of their house of origin, and some didn’t even get a hearing (https://calmatters.org/newsletters/whatmatters/2021/04/alex-lee-progressive-california/).
Meanwhile, Prop 42’s ban on retroactive state taxes — which includes an exemption for natural and fiscal emergencies — is also unnecessary and could create legal complications.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled in 1993 (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-512/pdf/USREPORTS-512-26.pdf) that retroactive taxes can be constitutional if “supported by a legitimate legislative purpose furthered by rational means.” The court determined the retroactive tax in question, which was “only slightly longer than one year,” was “modest” and met the standard.

Article continues below this ad
Yet Prop 42 outlaws any tax approved by the Legislature that applies more than one year retroactively — raising questions about how the measure might intersect with the standard set by the nation’s highest court.
Its true target is Prop 40, which would tax any billionaire living in California as of Jan. 1, 2026. And you don’t have to support the billionaire wealth tax to realize the potential collateral damage Prop 42 could cause.
If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no.

Now I have the full text of Prop 42. Key elements:

1. **Article VIII, Section 1**: No state law or constitutional provision enacted on or after Jan 1, 2026 may impose a tax on "ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" — defined extremely broadly to include ALL personal property, tangible or intangible (financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, IP, personal belongings, etc.).

2. Existing taxes (in effect and first collected on or before Dec 31, 2025) are grandfathered — so VLF, business personal property tax etc. remain.

3. **Section 2**: Prohibition on retroactive taxes — no state law enacted on or after Jan 1, 2026 may impose a tax that operates retroactively based on conduct, activities, or status that occurred before the effective date, including residency status before the effective date of the tax. Exception for emergency/fiscal emergency taxes applied retroactively no more than 365 days.

4. **Conflicting measures provision**: If Prop 42 gets more votes than another initiative on the same ballot that would impose a tax on ownership of personal property or retroactive tax (i.e., Prop 40), the other measure is null and void.

5. It only limits STATE taxes, not local taxes (the definition says "No state law and no provision of this Constitution...").

The SF Chronicle editorial notes:
- No one is coming for your 401(k); California follows federal framework of taxing on withdrawal.
- All six wealth tax proposals since 2019 died in the Legislature.
- Prop 40 excludes qualified pensions and retirement accounts (except mega-Roth IRAs > $10M).
- The retroactive ban could create legal complications relative to SCOTUS precedent (United States v. Carlton, 1993, allowing modest retroactive taxes).
- "Prop 42 papers over its real purpose by cynically appealing to middle-class worries about retirement security. Reject this appalling tactic... by voting no."
- Key point: "If you disagree with Prop 40, you can simply vote no." You don't need Prop 42 to kill Prop 40.

Now, what are the counter-arguments for Yes?
- Newsom and others argue a permanent ban is better protection than a one-time vote, because the Legislature could come back with another wealth tax next year.
- Firefighters/building trades argue it protects pensions/retirement from future politicians.
- The U-T and OC Register endorse it on limited-government grounds.
- Some economists oppose wealth taxes on capital-flight and efficiency grounds; Prop 42 enshrines that view.
- The ban on retroactive taxation addresses a real fairness concern (Prop 40's lookback to Jan 1, 2026 residency).

Weighing it all:

The core question: should I recommend Yes or No?

Considerations:

1. **Honest framing/deceptive intent**: Prop 42's stated purpose ("protect retirement savings") is not the real purpose. There is no proposal to tax ordinary retirement accounts. Prop 40, the actual target, only applies to billionaires and exempts retirement accounts. The campaign is funded by ~$100M+ from billionaires with direct financial stakes (Brin's estimated tax bill: $13 billion). The measure was written and funded by the very people it would benefit. Even the Sacramento Bee and LA Times column, which oppose Prop 40, oppose Prop 42 on these grounds.

2. **Policy merits on the merits**: Is a constitutional ban on personal property/wealth taxes good policy?
   - Pro: Prevents double taxation in principle; prevents retroactive taxes (a genuine fairness concern — Prop 40's retroactivity to Jan 1, 2026 residency is constitutionally questionable and arguably unfair); prevents capital flight incentives.
   - Con: Permanently forecloses a policy tool that ~190 other... well, no U.S. state currently has a wealth tax; the practical effect is minimal on ordinary Californians. The "threat" to retirement accounts is hypothetical. Six wealth tax bills have all died in the Legislature. So the protection is largely symbolic for ordinary people, while the real effect is shielding ~200 billionaires from a one-time tax and preventing future wealth taxes.
   - The emergency exception (365-day retroactive taxes in emergencies) is included, which mitigates some concerns.

3. **Process concerns**: Poison-pill/deception. Two redundant countermeasures (41, 42) designed to confuse; whichever gets more votes than Prop 40 kills it. A voter could sincerely support the idea "no taxes on retirement accounts" without realizing they're nullifying the billionaire tax. That's the definition of a deceptive measure. Editorial boards across the spectrum (Sac Bee — McClatchy, SF Chron — Hearst, Mercury News, LA Times) call this out.

4. **Who's on each side**: 
   - Yes: Brin + billionaires ($186M+), CalChamber, Reform California, firefighters/building trades/PORAC/AMVETS (some labor groups), Newsom, U-T, OCR.
   - No: SEIU-UHW, Bernie Sanders, California Democratic Party, Sac Bee, SF Chron, Mercury News.

5. **The strongest Yes argument**: If you oppose Prop 40 (as many do, including Newsom and several editorial boards), Prop 42 is insurance: even if Prop 40 passes, Prop 42 with more votes kills it AND prevents future wealth taxes. If you believe wealth taxes are bad policy and the Legislature will keep trying, a constitutional ban is more durable than defeating one initiative. Also, Prop 42's retroactivity ban addresses a real flaw in Prop 40 (taxing billionaires based on residency before the measure was even approved).

6. **The strongest No argument**: The measure is dishonestly marketed; its real-world effect is almost entirely to shield ~200 billionaires (many of whom already moved/shielded assets) from a one-time 5% tax; it would embed a broad, permanent constitutional restriction written by and for the ultra-wealthy; existing protections (all wealth tax bills dying, Prop 40's own exemptions, SCOTUS limits on retroactivity) already address the stated concerns; and if you oppose the billionaire tax, you can just vote No on Prop 40 — you don't need to amend the constitution with a deceptive poison-pill measure.

Now, how should I decide? The user wants a recommendation with a yes-or-no answer. I should weigh the evidence and give a clear answer with transparent reasoning.

Let me think about which side has the better case on the merits, considering I should be balanced.

Points in favor of No (my inclination):
- The measure's own ballot-title framing ("protect your retirement") misrepresents its primary effect. Independent analyses (LAO, CalMatters, Berkeley IGS guide, SF Chron, Sac Bee, LA Times) uniformly describe it as designed to nullify Prop 40.
- The problem it claims to solve (taxes on ordinary people's retirement accounts) does not exist: no enacted law, no live proposal beyond Prop 40 (which exempts retirement accounts and only applies to billionaires). Six prior wealth tax bills all died.
- The retroactivity concern: Prop 42's emergency exception is narrow; but also the only retroactive tax at issue is Prop 40 itself. So this provision is also aimed at Prop 40.
- Democratic legitimacy: If voters approve Prop 40 (majority), Prop 42 could nullify it with a conflicting majority — that's the same "will of the voters" logic both ways, but Prop 42 was specifically engineered so that voters who don't understand the interaction may inadvertently kill Prop 40. That's manipulative.
- Concentrated self-interest: ~$186M spent by ~a dozen billionaires with ~$1T+ combined wealth vs. ~$36M by supporters. This is among the most expensive initiative campaigns in U.S. history, and 90% is from the people the tax targets. Even people sympathetic to the anti-wealth-tax view (Skelton, Sac Bee) are repelled.
- Constitutional entrenchment of a policy preference written by interested billionaires is poor governance.

Points in favor of Yes:
- If the user is philosophically opposed to wealth taxes, this is the most robust way to prevent them.
- Retroactive taxation is genuinely odious; Prop 40's Jan 1, 2026 lookback is a real fairness problem (people made decisions before the rule existed). Prop 42 bans that practice going forward (with a 365-day emergency exception).
- The "slippery slope" argument: once a wealth tax exists for billionaires, the threshold could drop (e.g., to $50M millionaires). California has raised taxes repeatedly. Newsom's concern about capital flight is real — billionaire departure would reduce income tax revenue (top 1% pay ~half of income tax).
- The tax itself (Prop 40) has real problems: one-time windfall for ongoing spending, likely litigation, capital flight, and the possibility that the ~$100B projected doesn't materialize.
- Existing grandfathering means current taxes aren't affected.

Hmm. This is genuinely contested. But on balance, what's my recommendation?

Let me evaluate the strongest considerations:

1. **Deceptive purpose**: The single most important fact is that Prop 42's marketing ("protect your retirement") is a cover for its actual purpose (nullify the billionaire tax and ban wealth taxation). Every independent analyst acknowledges this. A voter should be able to trust that what a measure says it does is what it does. Measures that rely on misleading framing deserve skepticism.

2. **The stated problem doesn't exist**: There is no tax on ordinary retirement accounts, no live proposal for one, and the Legislature has repeatedly declined to pass wealth taxes. Prop 40 — the only live measure — exempts retirement accounts and applies only to ~200 billionaires. So for 99.9999% of Californians, Prop 42's "protection" is against a phantom threat.

3. **Retroactivity**: The only retroactive tax on the table is Prop 40's. If you oppose that, vote no on Prop 40. You don't need a constitutional amendment.

4. **Permanent policy lock-in via interested-party drafting**: The measure was drafted by billionaires' PAC. Even sympathetic observers (Sac Bee: "If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could..." — the quote got cut off, but suggests they might have tolerated it if narrower). The concern is "senselessly shackle the state's fiscal future."

5. **The counter-considerations are real but weaker**: 
   - Capital flight: a genuine concern about Prop 40, but the remedy is voting No on Prop 40.
   - Slippery slope: hypothetical; also, if the threshold ever dropped to affect ordinary people, the voters would have to approve it anyway (Prop 40 itself is an initiative; future wealth taxes by Legislature would face... actually the Legislature could pass a wealth tax with 2/3? No — tax increases require 2/3 legislative vote; and voters could repeal via initiative). The democratic process already provides checks.
   - Double taxation principle: This is a real philosophical argument ( taxing unrealized gains = taxing savings). But note Prop 40 taxes wealth, much of which is unrealized gains never taxed. One can debate. But the place to have that debate is on Prop 40 itself.

6. **Process/game-theory**: If Prop 42 fails and Prop 40 passes, we get the wealth tax. If you hate the wealth tax, that's bad. If Prop 42 passes and Prop 40 fails, no wealth tax and no wealth taxes ever. For a wealth-tax opponent, Prop 42 is strictly better. For a wealth-tax supporter, Prop 42 is strictly worse. For an undecided voter who distrusts the billionaire-funded deception, No is the choice.

So the vote on 42 essentially reduces to: do you want the billionaire tax to be possible or not, plus how much do you weigh the deceptive process?

Given that:
- The measure is deceptive by design (marketing a phantom threat to ordinary savers),
- Funded overwhelmingly (~90%) by the ~200 people who would directly benefit financially,
- Would nullify a separate measure voters may independently support, creating confusing outcomes,
- Amends the constitution to permanently ban a category of taxation based on a hypothetical threat,
- And its legitimate concerns (retroactivity, wealth tax flaws) can be addressed directly by voting No on Prop 40,

...the better recommendation is **No**.

I should present this with balance: acknowledge the genuine arguments for Yes (Newsom's, firefighters', the anti-wealth-tax philosophy, the retroactivity fairness point), but conclude No based on the deceptive framing, the phantom problem, self-interested funding, and the fact that the real policy question is decided on Prop 40 directly.

Also worth noting: even editorial boards that oppose Prop 40 (Sac Bee, LA Times/Skelton) recommend No on 42, calling it deceptive games-playing. The two papers endorsing Yes (U-T, OCR) do so on limited-government principle.

One more check: the user said "You can only answer yes or no." So my final answer must be a clear "No" (or "Yes"). I'll say "No" and explain. I should keep the answer reasonably concise but well-supported, given the instruction "Do extensive research before you answer." I've done the research; now I'll deliver a clear recommendation with the key reasoning, noting the one caveat: if their top priority is killing the wealth tax no matter what, they'd vote differently — but my recommendation is No.

Actually, let me do a bit more research to be thorough — check the Sac Bee full editorial, maybe the LA Times coverage of polls, and the fact-check on "could lawmakers expand the billionaire tax to everyone?" This is the key slippery-slope claim that would justify Yes. Let me check that fact-check.

Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Opponents of Proposition 40 have a message for voters: Don’t be fooled. The billionaire tax is a “Trojan horse” for new taxes on all Californians, ads proclaim (https://www.facebook.com/ads/library/?active_status=active&ad_type=all&country=US&id=1362825008785008&is_targeted_country=false&media_type=all&search_type=page&sort_data[mode]=total_impressions&sort_data[direction]=desc). But is that true? Tucked into the initiative is language granting the Legislature authority to amend the tax by a two-thirds vote “if the statute is consistent with and furthers the purposes of the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act.” Opponents argue lawmakers and a future governor could, with the stroke of a pen, expand the wealth tax to people with far less than $1 billion. In a high-tax state, that argument could hold a lot of sway with voters. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West put Prop. 40 on the ballot; the initiative would levy a one-time, 5% tax on billionaire’s assets. The union rejects the premise of the ad. It says the tax is limited to billionaires and any legislative amendment would have to hew closely to that purpose. Dave Regan, president of SEIU-UHW, said opponents’ ads are pure scare tactics. “The billionaire tax is a tax on billionaires. Period. If you’re not a billionaire, you don’t pay the tax,” Regan said in a statement to CalMatters. Rob Lapsley, president of the California Business Roundtable, the group that paid for the ad, said the message was meant to highlight the policy implications of a wealth tax and the power Prop. 40 gives lawmakers. “Californians deserve to understand those issues and what they could mean for taxpayers and the state’s economy,” Lapsley said in a statement. A separate, billionaire-backed group opposed to Prop. 40 has also said the initiative “gives politicians the power to expand the tax to anyone.” The truth lies somewhere in between. California courts have given lawmakers real authority to amend laws created by ballot initiatives if the original text of the initiative permits it. However, that power is not unlimited and the measure includes language restricting future legislative changes, said Michael Colantuono, an attorney with expertise in state election law. Opponents’ ads also don’t mention that Prop. 40 writes the tax into the state Constitution, not just state law, so expanding it would likely require another trip to the ballot. Legislative authority Legal experts agree that if Prop. 40 passes, lawmakers would be able to make certain amendments without taking it back to voters. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ The state Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS§ionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II) allows the Legislature to amend a ballot initiative without another vote if the initiative permits it. That’s a relatively common clause in ballot measures, and Prop. 40 includes it. Megan Jones, a tax attorney at Holland & Knight, said proponents’ claims that the tax could never be changed are disingenuous. “If it’s going to further the purposes, then they could,” Jones said. For example, voters passed the Political Reform Act, which governs campaign finance and lobbying rules, in 1974 and lawmakers have amended it almost continually since (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/the-law/the-political-reform-act/). Similarly, lawmakers have amended the Mental Health Services Act, a voter-approved 1% income tax on millionaires, 10 times since its passage in 2004. None of those amendments adjusted the tax rate. Most recently, lawmakers voted to substantially alter how the state spends mental health money and raise additional bond funds. Those changes went back to voters in 2024 as Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/). But there isn’t always a clear line for when voters need to approve changes, experts say. “It is common for the Legislature to make amendments,” Colantuono said. “It is (also) common for there to be disputes about those amendments.” ‘Furthers the purposes of’ “Ultimately, it ends up in court,” said Chris Parker, a principal tax attorney at the firm Baker Tilly. The California Supreme Court ruled in a 1995 case (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/4th/11/1243.html) that the Legislature may amend voter-approved laws if the changes can be interpreted as furthering voters’ original goals “by any reasonable construction” — giving lawmakers broad latitude. In 2021, the state Supreme Court held that the Legislature appropriately amended Proposition 57 (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2021/s259011.html), a criminal justice reform measure, by barring the transferring of minors under 16 to adult court. Justices cited the 1995 case, noting that “a strong presumption of constitutionality supports the Legislature’s acts.” Still, the language of the proposition matters. A few years earlier, in 2019, the Third District Court of Appeal held that a legislative attempt to allow public funding of political campaigns (https://www4.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/C086334.PDF) “directly conflicts with a primary purpose” of the Political Reform Act. Lawmakers responded by passing a new bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB42) asking voters to weigh in directly — it appears on this year’s ballot as Proposition 4. Judges look at two things, Coluantuono said: what reasonable voters thought they were approving, and whether later legislative changes helped that goal, or got in the way. Certain provisions of Prop. 40 would make it difficult for lawmakers to expand the tax beyond billionaires. The 1995 case established that courts may weigh the language of a ballot measure, arguments printed in the voter guide, and historical context when deciding whether change is consistent with voter intent. Prop. 40’s purpose and intent section (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop40-text-proposed-laws.pdf) says the measure is meant to support healthcare and education “by raising revenue from a one-time tax on billionaire wealth” — referencing billionaire wealth three times. The voter guide arguments similarly target “approximately 200 California billionaires.” “They could probably adjust the structure of the tax in marginal ways, but what they couldn’t do is make it a more than a one-time tax, and they probably couldn’t lower the threshold on wealth,” Coluantuono said. Opponents contend lawmakers could interpret the purpose of the act far more broadly, and a court would agree. They point to the first listed purpose of the initiative that says the tax is meant to “protect access to high quality, equitable health care, and to support funding for kindergarten through grade fourteen public education and food assistance programs.” Opponents also say the proposal gives the Legislature the authority to change all parts of the initiative, including the constitutional provisions. “Prop 40’s findings and statement of purpose and intent were carefully crafted to ensure that extending the tax to non-billionaires would be consistent with the measure,” said Kurt Oneto, a lawyer for the No on 40 campaign, in a statement. Experts said the question would likely come down to how a court read the act’s purposes. A separate concern: how do you prove wealth? Should Prop. 40 pass, it would create an entirely new tax structure in California — one that assigns a value to very wealthy people’s investments, public and private businesses, as well as personal property such as art or car collections. Valuing something like a tech startup that hasn’t produced a product or gone public could prove especially difficult, Parker said. “The excise tax that’s being proposed here is on potential,” he said. “The question then is, if we open the door to taxing potential, when does that stop?” Lawmakers have periodically tried to pass wealth taxes, but the bills quickly stalled. This marks the first time voters will directly decide on one, making Prop. 40 a crucial test of how much appetite Californians have for his kind of tax structure. Jones said the bigger worry isn’t the tax itself, but other taxes that could follow. “It’s a slippery slope,” she said. Coluantuono said it would still be politically risky for lawmakers to try to implement a wealth tax on everyday Californians, but history shows temporary taxes have more than once become permanent. “When we get a revenue stream in the government and we start spending it on services that people value… there’s tremendous political pressure to prevent the sunset,” he said. EDITORIAL: Endorsement: No on Props. 40, 41 and 42. Reject billionaires tax -- and billionaires' attempts to shackle state's fiscal future.
By East Bay Times
The Tribune Content Agency
Updated October 21, 2026 5:42 PM
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Successive waves of federal cuts to California's safety net are hitting our shores - and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California's Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state's safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 - countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state's fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It's the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here's how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state's 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised - estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert - would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn't just that it's targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They're difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn't fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley's largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California's extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state's income taxes.
For that reason, the state's most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst's Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will "probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax," according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That's because the LAO worries that "billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away."
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state's General Fund revenues by "less than a billion per year."
But the union that pushed this proposition - Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West - wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they'll suffer when the state's General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
"We can't let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state's tax code on its own terms," said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn't agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California - a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt - created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won't take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative's requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor's recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the "Gann Limit" - a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.
California has changed radically since the 1970s. And its fiscal rules must leave the state with the flexibility to address issues voters of the era never had to deal with - six-figure college costs, seven-figure mortgages and 13-figure wildfire costs.
The state must not surrender its future freedom of action to defeat a single, one-time tax proposal.
Proposition 42
This initiative would prohibit the state from taxing retroactively. And it would permanently ban the state from any new taxes on ownership of financial assets or other personal properties - think stocks, bonds, intellectual property, artwork, etc.
Taxes on wealth are rarely ideal, and our opposition to Proposition 40 reflects that.
However, we are witnessing an explosion of inequality, and the unpredictable course of AI's development risks supercharging the gap between the haves and have-nots. Joint Venture Silicon Valley's latest research shows that 78% of Bay Area residents are concerned AI will increase economic inequality.
Proposition 42 was written by this tech boom's beneficiaries, who are now among the wealthiest humans in history. If this initiative had limited itself to nullifying Proposition 40, we could have supported it. However, amid this era's technology- and climate-induced uncertainty, California must keep its options open.
Proposition 42 would needlessly and recklessly narrow them.
Reject Propositions 40, 41 and 42.
